prompt: Write a short blog post about the first harvest of the year. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# The First Harvest

There's a particular kind of quiet that settles over the garden in the weeks before the first harvest. The seeds are in, the seedlings have been hardened off, and all that's left is waiting. I'm not a patient person by nature, but gardening has been slowly teaching me.

This morning, the wait ended.

I went out just after sunrise, still in my slippers, coffee in one hand and a battered colander in the other. The grass was soaked with dew, and the air had that cool, green smell that only exists in the first hour of the day. I wasn't planning to pick anything. I only meant to check on things. But there, tucked under a canopy of leaves, were the radishes, their shoulders pushing up out of the soil like little red knuckles.

I pulled one. It came free with a satisfying tug, trailing a tangle of fine roots and a clump of dark earth. I rinsed it under the hose, took a bite right there in the yard, and nearly laughed out loud. It was sharp, peppery, and crisp, nothing like the sad, waxy ones from the grocery store. Eight weeks of watering, weeding, and worrying, all packed into one bite.

Next came the lettuce. I'd sown it thickly, as I always do, and it had rewarded my carelessness with ruffled green rosettes. I snipped the outer leaves with kitchen scissors, leaving the hearts to keep growing. A handful of spinach joined them, then a few sprigs of chives that had somehow survived the winter and decided to show off.

By the time I finished, the colander held maybe two pounds of produce. It isn't much. You couldn't feed a family on it. But there's something about the first harvest that has nothing to do with quantity. It's proof. It tells you that the strange bargain you made with the soil, that you'd show up and it would respond, actually works.

I carried everything inside and laid it out on the counter like treasure. Lunch was a simple salad with olive oil, lemon, salt, and a few shaved radishes on top. I ate it slowly, on the back step, watching the bees work the chive blossoms.

There will be bigger harvests. Tomatoes will come, then squash in absurd, unmanageable quantities, and I'll be leaving zucchini on neighbors' porches by August. But I suspect none of them will taste quite like this first one, the one that reminded me why I started.

If you've been thinking about planting something, anything, do it. Even a pot of radishes on a windowsill will do. The reward is bigger than the effort, and the wait is shorter than you think.

Now, if you'll excuse me, I need to go check on the peas.
